items.body:
TBCo is stepping into the AW season with a renewed sense of purpose and an exciting expansion. Known for its colourful homeware, joyful palette and cult-status accessories, TBCo will launch into Harrods for the first time this October with their signature accessories line, pyjamas and robes.
TBCo continues its evolution from product-led heritage to full lifestyle brand with purpose-driven values and bold creative direction. As a certified B Corp, the brand balances playful, high-quality design with natural and recycled fibres. The AW26 collection brings together whimsical, soft and elevated designs throughout their sleep offering that feels luxurious for slow mornings and dreamlike getaways. Designed in Edinburgh and brought to life by a dedicated team of creatives, TBCo’s collections are grounded in a belief that sustainability and style can, and should, go hand in hand.
The launch into Harrods marks an exciting milestone for the brand as they continue their global expansion and category offering. Harrods will stock a variety of the brand’s key pieces from their AW collection including their best selling Merino wool triangle scarves in brown and blue & pink and burgundy. Alongside their sleep offering with a wide range of pyjamas in tartan, check, bold stripes and deep burgundys along with their bestselling Terry Cotton Robes.
“We are thrilled to be launching TBCo in Harrods, sleepwear is a category we see so much growth and demand from our customers for. With gifting seasons around the corner we know that the playful colours and modern designs will really bring joy to our customers,” said Clemmie Harris, head of buying, fashion at Harrods.
“Launching TBCo sleepwear and accessories at Harrods is a significant milestone for the brand. Harrods has always represented the epitome of luxury and quality to me, so seeing our collections alongside such an exceptional line-up of brands is a proud moment and a reflection of how far TBCo has grown. Our distinctive colour and pattern bring something unique to the department, combining expressive design with beautiful quality and pieces that bring joy to the everyday. This launch marks an exciting next chapter in our journey as we continue to grow TBCo as a design-led fashion and lifestyle brand,” said Emma Macdonald, founder and CEO of TBCo.TBCo will be available to shop in store on floor 1 in the Harrods Lingerie & Lounge room from October, 2026.

items.title: Fed questions whether falling shop theft figures tell the full story
items.summary: The Federation of Independent Retailers (the Fed) has questioned whether the latest government figures accurately reflect the true scale of shop theft, warning that recorded offences do not tell the full story of the crime experienced by independent retailers. The latest figures issued by the… This story continues at Fed questions whether falling shop theft figures tell the full story Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The latest figures issued by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show that recorded shop theft fell by 2% in the year ending June 2026, with 519,516 offences compared with 530,336 the previous year.
National president Hemanshu Patel said: “While the figures show a fall in recorded shop theft, we need to understand whether this reflects a genuine reduction in crime or whether it also reflects the difficulties retailers face when reporting incidents and the lack of confidence some have in the process.
“More than half a million recorded offences in a single year remains a serious concern. Behind these figures are independent retailers dealing with repeated theft, intimidation and the financial and emotional impact of crime. The wider impact on staff, customers and local communities must not be overlooked.”
In a statement issued by the Home Office, policing minister Sarah Jones said: “Police are taking this crime seriously, and with more officers patrolling town centres and responding to these incidents we can have a real impact.
“Shop theft charge rates rose from 19% to 24%. This is still too low, and we want to see this figure continue to climb. We will continue this trend by pushing ahead with plans to strengthen local policing.”
Patel added: “We welcome the minister’s recognition that shop theft charge rates remain too low. However, retailers need to see meaningful action on the ground, not simply changes in the statistics.
“Reporting crime must be straightforward, police responses must be appropriate and offenders must understand there are consequences for their actions. Retailers should not have to navigate unnecessary red tape only to feel that little is being done.
“We also want the government to consider a dedicated retail crime grant scheme to help independent retailers improve security and protect their businesses.
“Recorded figures are only part of the picture. Independent retailers deserve to feel safe, supported and properly protected.”

items.title: Sainsbury’s grows faster than Tesco in H1, but its sales momentum is fading, says GlobalData
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Following today’s release of Sainsbury’s figures for the 28 weeks ending 12 September 2026; Eleanor Simpson-Gould, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Sainsbury’s has outpaced Tesco on sales growth in H1, but weak non-food sales continue to hold back an otherwise strong food performance. Sales from continuing […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Following today’s release of Sainsbury’s figures for the 28 weeks ending 12 September 2026; Eleanor Simpson-Gould, senior retail analyst at GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform, offers her view: “Sainsbury’s has outpaced Tesco on sales growth in H1, but weak non-food sales continue to hold back an otherwise strong food performance. Sales from continuing operations (excluding fuel) rose 2.6% to £14.0bn, driven by a 4.3% rise in fresh food sales and continued trade-up to Taste the Difference. Like-for-like (l-f-l) sales rose 1.9%, ahead of Tesco’s 1.5%. However, momentum slowed sharply through the first half, from 2.3% in Q1 to 1.2% in Q2, against tough comparatives and easing food inflation. Sainsbury’s raised the lower end of its full-year underlying operating profit guidance to £1,025m, matching Tesco’s cautious upgrade earlier this month. Shares fell close to 4% in morning trading, likely reflecting this caution alongside plans to keep investing in value, quality, availability and service through a very competitive second half.
“The agreed sale of Argos to Swift Partners is the defining change of the half. Argos, now a discontinued operation, saw sales fall 1.8% in H1, worsening to a 2.7% decline in Q2. Big-ticket furniture sales stalled in the heatwave, and the move away from legacy Argos credit cards weighed on sales. Selling Argos removes a volatile drag for the grocer and will free Sainsbury’s to focus capital and strategy on food, but non-food will remain a weak spot. Sainsbury’s general merchandise and clothing sales decreased by 3.4%, largely due to a deliberate shift of space towards food. The 13% rise in toy sales after a range reset shows that fewer, better ranges can still grow sales going into the gifting season. However, Argos will still trade this Christmas under Sainsbury’s ownership, so a weak golden quarter will further hamper Sainsbury’s performance. Sainsbury’s must keep the separation, due in February 2029, tightly managed so that it does not distract from the core business.
“Grocery sales rose 2.9% to £13.2bn, with Aldi Price Match and Nectar Prices on almost 11,000 products driving growth in the half. Premium remains central to growth. Taste the Difference sales grew by more than 6%, and the restaurant-quality Discovery range doubled, driving a quarter of that growth. With the Middle East conflict continuing to put pressure on energy costs and inflation set to rise into Sainsbury’s H2, the grocer must protect volumes over Christmas and retain focus on price matching. It should lead with fewer, higher-impact Discovery and Taste the Difference festive lines and use Nectar Prices to lower the barrier to trying them.”

items.title: Tax online sales more heavily to save high streets, Burnham urged
items.summary: Exclusive: British Chambers of Commerce president calls for overhaul of business rates and greater powers for local leaders How Middleton’s revival could inspire struggling towns What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients Andy Burnham has been urged by one of his most senior former advisers to tax internet sales more heavily than in-store purchases to help “level the playing field” for struggling high streets. As the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, prepare for their first budget next week, Andy Haldane joined calls for action to stop more shops closing across the UK. Continue reading...
items.body:
Andy Burnham has been urged by one of his most senior former advisers to tax internet sales more heavily than in-store purchases to help “level the playing field” for struggling high streets.
As the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, prepare for their first budget next week, Andy Haldane joined calls for action to stop more shops closing across the UK.
In an interview for a Guardian series looking at how Britain can reverse the declining fortunes of towns, the former Bank of England chief economist urged them to launch a realignment of the tax system away from favouring online sellers, alongside a review of business rates and measures to turbocharge devolution.
“The balance of tax incentives are strongly skewed towards the digital over the physical, and the large over small, and if you’re serious about high streets that needs somehow rebalancing,” he said.
Calling on Burnham to follow through with Labour’s manifesto promise to “replace” the business rates system, Haldane said “some levelling of the playing field” was needed to help smaller operators who faced soaring costs and evaporating demand.
“One of the reasons why high streets are dying, and some of the towns, is business rates are punitive for smaller shops,” he said. “This needs to be wrapped up with that more fundamental review of business rates and I’ll hope we see that in the budget.
The prime minister has made town centres a top priority after years of decline that have left many hollowed-out, with shops closed, buildings boarded up and once-busy hubs sitting empty.
Healey’s budget on Wednesday is tipped to include measures to ease the pressure on these high streets, including a tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay. The measure could raise up to an extra £1bn by forcing them to collect VAT on behalf of large-scale sellers based in the UK as well as those overseas.
He is also expected to honour the promise Burnham made in June to take more small players out of the system altogether by raising the rent valuation threshold at which businesses start paying.
The Treasury is also understood to have taken an interest in a report by the IPPR thinktank calling for an online sales tax to fund lower high street business rates. Big retailers including Morrisons, Waterstones and the UK’s biggest supermarket, Tesco, have long called for such a move.
Labour has already had one business rates shake-up. In April, taxes on warehouses used by online retailers were increased, but the increase on the UK’s most valuable commercial properties also drew other large buildings such as department stores and hotels fuelling calls for further tweaks. Some retailers have warned against a more targeted warehouse tax because many big chains now combine online shopping with a high-street presence.
Allen Simpson, the boss of the trade body UKHospitality, said the government had indicated it would ease costs on his sector, but he sensed ministers were wary of US retribution if taxes on big US-based tech firms such as Amazon and eBay were hit, warning that “Trump might hit us with a tariff”.
Burnham’s push to revive communities with measures to hand more power and money to local leaders comes as Nigel Farage’s Reform UK seeks to weaponise high-street decline. Research shows public support for his rightwing populist party has grown most in the places where high-street vacancy rates have risen most.
Haldane, who is the president of the British Chambers of Commerce, advised Burnham as he prepared to enter Downing Street but did not take a formal position in government.
A leading expert in regional economic development who masterminded Boris Johnson’s levelling up plans – before distancing himself from the Conservatives over cuts to local government – he praised Burnham’s agenda to hand more power and funding to local leaders. However, Haldane said a revamp of business rates would be critical to boosting the economies of struggling towns. “That would be a very, very important element of the ‘growth in every postcode’, and making the most of devolution outside the city centric mayoralties,” he said.
In his first weeks in power Burnham announced a cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April. Labour has also introduced community ownership funds and launched a £5.8bn “pride in place” strategy to hand more money and power to local leaders to support regeneration.
However, retail and hospitality industry leaders argue that Labour has added to the headwinds facing high streets by increasing taxes on employment and adding to other business costs, and have pressed for these to be partly reversed to fund youth job creation.
As ministers prepare to publish a refreshed high streets strategy, polling by researchers at More in Common shared with the Guardian by the campaign group Power to Change shows the extent of the challenge.
Whereas most people describe their local area warmly, opinions typically turn negative when asked about their high street, with words like “empty”, “run down,” “tired” and “declining” common.
As many as six in 10 think handing more power to community organisations, residents or local businesses would help to improve their high street. As few as 15% thought the government would make better decisions.
Haldane urged Labour to hand more powers to directly elected mayors – including the eventual responsibility for setting local rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT. “Other countries have cracked the code on this. So there’s no reason why we couldn’t or shouldn’t,” he said.
Healey is preparing to use the budget to unveil plans to allow mayors to retain a share of income tax but is expected to stop short of handing over the responsibilities from the Treasury to set local rates.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “We are on the side of businesses. The chancellor is giving the high street more breathing space, cutting business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues. This is alongside £4.3bn to limit bill rises, funded by a higher tax rate for big online warehouses, and capping corporation tax.
“As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

items.title: How Middleton’s revival could be grist to the mill for Britain’s struggling towns
items.summary: Turnaround initiated by Andy Burnham and led by Steve Coogan could provide blueprint for other neglected areas Save high street by taxing online sales at higher rate, Burnham urged What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients The former England footballer Paul Scholes and the actor Steve Coogan stare out from beside a fish and chip shop in Middleton, near Manchester . Looming over a mural of the pair – and the whole town – is an enormous former cotton mill that powered its economy a century ago. The deafening looms and spindles of Warwick Mill fell silent decades ago, replaced in recent years by TikTok “urban explorers” who share videos of themselves crawling through its abandoned shell. Continue reading...
items.body:
The former England footballer Paul Scholes and the actor Steve Coogan stare out from beside a fish and chip shop in Middleton, near Manchester. Looming over a mural of the pair – and the whole town – is an enormous former cotton mill that powered its economy a century ago.
The deafening looms and spindles of Warwick Mill fell silent decades ago, replaced in recent years by TikTok “urban explorers” who share videos of themselves crawling through its abandoned shell.
Yet the old building may have life inside it yet: last month Rochdale council wrestled Warwick Mill out of the hands of its absentee owner, a millionaire Chinese businessman, under whom it had been derelict for years.
Now the Grade II-listed site is at the centre of plans Andy Burnham believes could turn Middleton, where he was once a trainee journalist, into a blueprint for the future of Britain’s struggling towns.
“It used to be good,” said Dorothy Kersh, in the town square with her husband, Ernie, both 83. “In the 70s we had a cinema, we had banks. It’s lost character and we’ve hardly got any shops. We haven’t even got a bank now – I never thought NatWest would leave Middleton. It’s just going downhill.”
A few miles between Manchester and Rochdale, Middleton is typical of the existential crisis suffered by most British towns.
A decade or so ago, locals could find virtually everything they needed in its neat square of grocers, butchers and banks. But a giant Tesco has hoovered up the cash since it opened in 2013, compounding the rise of online and out-of-town shopping.
The town of about 50,000 people has lost all its banks and, days before Burnham became prime minister, the remains of its post office were closed by Modella Capital, the new private equity owner of WH Smith.
Now the shopping precinct offers little more than bookmakers, vape stores, pawnbrokers and fast-food outlets.
Even its geographic identity feels muddled. Middleton was historically in Lancashire but the town has a Manchester postcode and dial code, although residents pay their council tax to Rochdale. The region’s lauded tram network does not stop here.
“It’s really a dying town,” said Tim King, outside a large post office branch that closed down years ago. “We’ve only got one cash machine and that’s at Tesco, and there’s never any money in it. We’ve lost out on the trams. We haven’t got anything down here, to be honest.”
But six miles from the birthplace of the modern co-operative movement in 1844, a community fightback is under way.
Months before he departed for Downing Street, Burnham launched a mayoral development corporation for Middleton, giving local leaders power to set lower business rates, acquire underused land and property, and build 1,500 new homes.
The body is led by Coogan, the Bafta-winning creator of Alan Partridge, and Rose Marley, the chief executive of Co-operatives UK. Crucially, residents and business owners will have a seat at the table: a survey of 2,000 Middletonians is shaping the agenda of this new mayoral body – with Warwick Mill and other empty buildings identified by locals as an immediate priority.
Wearing a hard hat and hi-vis vest during a tour of Warwick Mill last month, Coogan said the Middleton of his childhood was a “thriving” town but that “over the last 35 years there has been a kind of a bank ride” by firms registered in the British Virgin Islands, China and the US: “All that money has been extracted but very little has been put back into the infrastructure.”
Coogan said the project was about more than attempting to revitalise his home town. It was a chance to reverse the political and economic malaise that has seen former Labour voters shift to rightwing populist parties such as Reform UK in post-industrial areas across Britain.
“There’s a problem in this country which is post-industrial neglect,” he told the Guardian. “The idea, the Blairite approach: it’s called multinationalism, there is nothing we can do, throw your hands up, you’ve just got to see what happens, we can’t help these people.
“Leaving that vacuum will mean that the extremists, populist extremists, will fill that gap. That’s the problem with top-down, well-meaning, but disempowering, philanthropic, centralised socialism. People don’t want to receive charity, they want to be empowered.”
Coogan is part of a group called Middleton Co-operating, which aims to “rewire the whole of the economy locally” by taking infrastructure and everyday essentials into public control.
Its plans include using renewable energy, like solar panels and small wind turbines, to help power a secondary school and a hospice. A trial involving heat pumps and solar panels on a terrace of Edwardian homes is also being put together.
Banks could soon return too, with plans for a banking hub where Lloyds, NatWest and others could open on different days of the week, alongside financial advisers.
The group, which was backed by Burnham when he was mayor and in June won £4.5m funding from the national lottery’s solidarity fund, wants to expand into food production, early years support, mental health provision and adult social care.
“These are all things that have the biggest impact on people’s day-to-day lives and they’re generally all owned by big business and private equity – they cost too much and are a cause of a lot of stress in the community,” said Mark Fraser, a founder of Middleton Co-operating.
Earlier this year, an arts venue run by Middleton Co-operating was forced out of the town’s sprawling shopping centre – which was owned by two London-based real estate companies and incorporated in the British Virgin Islands – as it could not afford the £43,000-a-year rent and service charge demanded by the landlord. In its place a pawnbroker moved in on a 10-year lease.
“It was a bit of a sickener,” said Fraser. “It was a lesson in that they were saying they loved what we were doing for the community, but when it came to it what counts is the bottom line.”
Even with Coogan’s star power and the prime minister’s backing, the scale of the challenge is huge.
Warwick Mill is an utter wreck and could cost tens of millions of pounds to bring back to life. To Fraser, it is a symbol of a town where people feel “neglected and forgotten”, and most had lost hope in its future.
“The cost of rescuing and converting something of that size is colossal,” said Tim Heatley, the co-founder of property firm Capital & Centric, which specialises in turning unloved old buildings – such as former mills and even multistorey car parks – into sought-after homes.
It was a 7pm telephone call from Burnham that turned Heatley on to Warwick Mill in January this year.
The then mayor told Heatley he had seen Capital & Centric’s renovation of the dilapidated Weir Mill in Stockport and asked him to take a look at the Middleton site.
As it happened, Heatley had already been in contact with Kam Lei Fong, the Macau-based developer who owned Warwick Mill. But with Burnham on board, the project accelerated.
“For me, the opportunity is much bigger than doing a nice conversion of an old mill,” he said. “Warwick is absolutely colossal and has loomed over Middleton for more than a century. If we can fill it with life again, it has the potential to become an anchor for the town … and give confidence for investment to follow around it.
“The challenge now is turning all that momentum into an actual place, getting Warwick fixed up, full of people and properly part of Middleton again. Ideally before Andy’s next career move leaves us needing to find somebody else to cut the ribbon.”

items.title: Supermarket giants welcome crackdown on Aldi and Lidl
items.summary: Supermarket giants, including Waitrose and Morrisons, have welcomed the competition watchdog’s decision to crack down on Aldi and Lidl. Lidl and Aldi are currently excluded from a law which bans the UK’s biggest supermarket chains from engaging in so-called ‘landblocking‘. Top grocers have already warned that the existing rules allowed the two German discounters to use a “problematic” [...]
items.body:
Supermarket giants welcome crackdown on Aldi and Lidl
Supermarket giants, including Waitrose and Morrisons, have welcomed the competition watchdog’s decision to crack down on Aldi and Lidl.
Lidl and Aldi are currently excluded from a law which bans the UK’s biggest supermarket chains from engaging in so-called ‘landblocking‘. Top grocers have already warned that the existing rules allowed the two German discounters to use a “problematic” loophole to block rivals from opening nearby.
However, the competition regulator is now set to force the two grocers to comply.
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) on Thursday confirmed its provisional decision to extend the Controlled Land Order to cover Aldi and Lidl.
The pair had previously been excluded from the rules because they were classed as “limited assortment discounters”. But the CMA has said it will now categorise the two firms as “large grocery retailers” because of their rapid expansion in recent years.
Lidl and Aldi will join Asda, Co-op, Marks & Spencer, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose in being blocked from using these land laws to gain an advantage over their rivals.
Budget supermarket Iceland, which is not covered by the land order, welcomed the CMA’s provisional decision.
In a letter to the regulator, published on Thursday, the company said existing rules allowed Aldi and Lidl to “deploy problematic land arrangements […] at scale and in a way that could have a material adverse impact on competition for groceries across the UK market”.
Though the two German discounters occupied a relatively small part of the UK’s grocery market when the Controlled Land Order was set up, the firms “now each exert a significant and compelling degree of competitive influence in the UK grocery market,” Iceland said.
Lidl and Aldi ‘shielded from competition’
Grocers Morrisons, Waitrose and Iceland each wrote to the CMA, expressing concerns that Lidl and Aldi are preparing to expand further in the UK, citing plans to reach 1,500 stores each.
Aldi and Lidl have previously claimed they should not be classed as large grocery retailers because they offer fewer products than their rivals.
But Morrisons told the CMA that both supermarket chains “publicly market their product range as being suitable for a full weekly shop” and pose “intense competition” even in the categories they claim to be weak in.
A Waitrose spokesperson wrote to the regulator, warning that it had seen “first hand” Lidl’s use of the land order to “restrict the ability of other grocery retailers to open new stores and shield Lidl from local competition”.
The up-market grocer said the CMA should impose its rulings as soon as possible. “It is important that these decisions are taken without further delay to ensure there is equal opportunity in the competition between LGRs and Aldi and Lidl to secure further sites for grocery retail.”
Juliette Enser, executive director for competition enforcement at the regulator, said the new rules will “help level the playing field and make sure shoppers get the best choice of products and prices in their area”.
Responding to the CMA’s provisional ruling in August, Lidl and Aldi said the crackdown would not slow their plans to expand rapidly in the UK.
Commenting on the decision, an Aldi spokesperson said: “We remain firmly committed to opening hundreds of new stores across the country, bringing Aldi’s unbeatable value and award-winning quality to even more customers.
A Lidl spokesperson said: “As a discounter, we have always welcomed and embraced competition within the market, and our focus remains on continuing to open new stores and bringing our high-quality, lowest-priced groceries to even more communities.”

items.title: Primark announces AI powered supply chain decision capability partnership with Kallikor
items.summary: Primark has partnered with Kallikor to introduce a simulation led approach to supply chain decisions. The aim being for the retailer to test and validate operational and capital changes before implementation.The tie up begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing te
items.body:
Primark has partnered with Kallikor to introduce a simulation led approach to supply chain decisions. The aim being for the retailer to test and validate operational and capital changes before implementation.
The tie up begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing teams to test alternative operating configurations before implementation.
By comparing scenarios in a simulated environment, the retailer says it can identify more efficient approaches while protecting customer service and avoiding downstream cost or operational impacts across the store estate.
Adam Hoccom, Director of Supply Chain at Primark, says: “As we continue to grow across markets, ensuring our supply chain is designed to support that ambition is critical."
"A key part of that is making sure our distribution centres operate efficiently while remaining aligned to store needs. Working with Kallikor allows us to test and compare different operating configurations - from layout and flow changes within sites to broader network considerations - before we commit capital spend."
"This gives us greater confidence in the choices we make and how they will perform in practice, strengthening our ability to innovate and make well-informed decisions as we evolve our network.”
By modelling operational flows in detail - from pick paths and labour constraints to throughput variability and service impacts - Primark can see how proposed changes will perform in practice before they are introduced. The models are built from its operational data, with the aim of ensuring outcomes reflect how the system actually performs under a range of real operating conditions rather than relying on assumptions or averaged views of the network.
The modelling also establishes a living decision environment built on Primark’s operational data that can be reused and extended as new strategic questions arise. Rather than commissioning a new analysis for each decision, teams can continuously test alternatives within the same validated model as the supply chain evolves.
Through simulation and AI enabled scenario exploration, they can run and compare multiple operating futures side-by-side, assessing trade offs across cost, service, capacity and risk in parallel.
Jack O’Connell, CEO and Co-Founder at Kallikor, says: “At Primark’s scale, no supply chain decision exists in isolation. A change in one distribution centre can affect capacity, flow, service and performance across the wider network. Our role is to help teams explore decisions that would otherwise carry too much uncertainty, testing different scenarios before implementation so leaders can understand the trade-offs and move forward with confidence."
"We’re proud to support Primark as they build a simulation led decision-making capability, beginning with their distribution centres and creating the foundations for better decisions across the wider supply chain over time.”

items.title: Sainsbury’s expects challenging run-up to Christmas as households feel squeeze
items.summary: Supermarket urges government not to ‘further aggravate’ pressure on costs for businesses in next week’s budget Sainsbury’s has warned of a “pretty challenging” market in the run-up to Christmas as households are “finding it tough” and food producers face rising costs. Simon Roberts, the chief executive of the UK’s second biggest supermarket, called on the government not to “further aggravate” pressure on costs for business in this month’s budget. He said it was “important this government does not repeat what we have seen in previous budgets” in raising business rates and employers’ national insurance contributions. “That’s been really hard,” he said. Continue reading...
items.body:
Sainsbury’s has warned of a “pretty challenging” market in the run-up to Christmas as households are “finding it tough” and food producers face rising costs.
Simon Roberts, the chief executive of the UK’s second biggest supermarket, called on the government not to “further aggravate” pressure on costs for business in this month’s budget. He said it was “important this government does not repeat what we have seen in previous budgets” in raising business rates and employers’ national insurance contributions. “That’s been really hard,” he said.
After Sainsbury’s and other industry leaders met government ministers last week, Roberts said he believed “this government is really listening to business” especially on helping to create more jobs for young people.
Roberts added that food inflation was not “anything like” some of the high levels forecast earlier in the year but suggested high energy and fertiliser costs could push up food prices next year.
Roberts said that in a more unsettled global environment the UK needed to “improve food resilience and grow and produce more at home”. He called on the government to increase tax breaks that support investment in technology – including irrigation and reservoirs – on farms, as the climate crisis is expected to lead to more hotter, drier summers such as this year’s.
Shares in Sainsbury’s fell by about 3% on Thursday as the retailer revealed slower than expected sales growth of 2.6% in the six months to 12 September, with growth almost halving to 1.9% in the second quarter from 3% in the first. Strong online grocery sales – up 9% – and a 6% rise in sales of the retailer’s premium own-label Taste the Difference range helped with growth.
Roberts said sales had slowed as shoppers had kept a tight rein on the number of items they bought because of a “focus on the cost of living” and had reduced spending on clothing and “big-ticket” items, such as furniture, at Argos. Sales at the catalogue shop were down 1.8% and Sainsbury’s general merchandise and clothing sales were down 3.4% in the half.
The growth figures for grocery and clothing were also dented by comparison with last summer, when Sainsbury’s and other retailers experienced a boost to trade after Marks & Spencer and the Co-op were affected by cyber-attacks.
Pre-tax losses for the half year widened to £63m from £14m a year before. However, the company reported a 5.2% rise in underlying profit to £366m, excluding the Argos catalogue shop, which is in the process of being sold off. The deal is expected to complete in February and the businesses to be totally separated by 2029.
Sainsbury’s said it now expects an annual underlying profit of at least £1.02bn, slightly more than the £975m previously outlined.
Charles Allen, a senior retail analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said the figures suggested Sainsbury’s was not expecting to increase profits in the second half of the year against a “tougher competitive backdrop as inflation returns and rivals prioritise sales growth”.
Roberts refused to comment on speculation that Sainsbury’s was set to buy one of its rivals – amid reports that it had entered, and ended, talks to buy Morrisons earlier this year.
However, the group said it planned to open 10 supermarkets and 25 convenience stores by March, which some analysts said reduced the need to seek a merger with a rival.

items.title: ACS highlights increasingly violent shop theft in latest crime figures
items.summary: The Association of Convenience Stores (ACS) has responded to new national figures on crime from the Office for National Statistics, which have shown that thieves are increasingly threatening violence against retailers and shopworkers. The latest Crime Survey for England and Wales, released today (22 October)… This story continues at ACS highlights increasingly violent shop theft in latest crime figures Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The latest Crime Survey for England and Wales, released today (22 October) shows a 2% fall in the number of shop thefts recorded by the police in the year to June 2026.
However, this comes alongside a 10% increase in the number of robberies recorded.
The reason for the marked increase in robberies is likely due to a change in the way that some offences are now recorded as robberies that previously would have been counted as shoplifting offences.
From the ONS’ notes on the release: “If an offender enters a retail premises, steals, and either uses or threatens violence against a shop worker, or security guard, or any other person at the time, or uses or threatens violence to escape, then an offence of robbery of business property should be recorded.
“This clarification is likely to also have had a small effect on reducing the number of shoplifting offences.”
The convenience retail body has welcomed the change in recording as it means that offences of this nature will be treated more seriously by forces and face tougher penalties as a result, but has urged caution over claims that theft is falling overall.
ACS chief executive Ed Woodall said: “We are extremely concerned about the changing nature of theft against retailers. Offenders are becoming more confident, more brazen, and ultimately more violent in their crimes, threatening retailers and shopworkers to get away with stolen goods.
“The Crime and Policing Act marked a big step forward in ensuring that the police treat shop theft more seriously, but many of the key measures from the Act such as the scrapping of the £200 threshold for investigating thefts, and the separate offence for attacking a shopworker are still not in place.
“The government must act as soon as possible to show that it backs the hardworking people running and working in our nation’s local shops.”

items.title: Selfridges unveils Christmas windows with festive scenes from around the world
Retail industry welcomes shoplifting decrease with caution
items.summary: The latest ONS crime stats show that, following a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 2% decrease (to 519,516 offences) in the year ending June 2026, when compared with the previous year (530,336 offences). Recent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect… This story continues at Retail industry welcomes shoplifting decrease with caution Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Recent increases in police recorded shoplifting likely reflect both growth in offences and improved reporting resulting from closer engagement between police and retailers.
Reporting rates for shoplifting are known to be very low and police are actively encouraging the reporting of all incidents and the submission of supporting evidence, such as CCTV, to strengthen intelligence, identify offenders, and link related offences.
The Crime Survey for England and Wales also show a 10% increase in the overall number of robbery offences recorded.
Responding to the figures, Lucy Whing, crime policy adviser at the British Retail Consortium (BRC), said: “Retailers will welcome today’s figures, but progress on tackling shop theft is still too slow.
“Theft is not a victimless crime: it fuels violence against shop workers, and adds costs that ultimately hit shoppers’ pockets. With 1,600 incidents of violence or abuse against retail workers every day, the human toll remains unacceptable.
“The Crime and Policing Act granted police new powers to intervene and prosecute offenders, including a long-overdue offence of assaulting a retail worker. Yet six months after the new law passed, these protections have still not come into force.
“Retail workers face abuse every day – their safety must not be the price of government inaction.
“A nationwide week of action against retail crime begins on 9 November, bringing together police, retailers and government in a united effort to tackle offending.
“Ministers should seize the moment to announce the commencement date for these new protections, giving retail workers the reassurance they need and sending a clear message that violence and theft on our streets will not be tolerated.”
Chris Brook-Carter, chief executive of retail industry charity the Retail Trust, said: “The small reduction in retail crime is another sign that combined efforts by the government, police and retailers are starting to make a difference, but there is still much more to do before people working on the frontline of retail feel genuinely safer and happier at work.
“Today’s figures don’t yet the reflect the reality of many of the shop workers we speak to, who tell us their confidence, wellbeing and sense of safety are being damaged by daily incidents of theft, violence and abuse.
“This is at the same time that our latest Retail People Index shows four in 10 staff are at already risk of working while unwell and nearly half are considering leaving their jobs.
“The stronger protections for shop staff being introduced as part of the Crime and Policing Act are also welcome steps towards dealing with persistent offenders and serious crime. But these measures alone won’t bring an end to the everyday hostility, intimidation and verbal abuse that too many shop workers face, and which often goes unreported.
“The improvements we’re seeing in recorded shop theft now need to be backed by consistent enforcement, better reporting processes and more practical training and wellbeing support to help staff respond to and recover from incidents.
“Every one of us also needs to play our part in challenging the attitudes that have allowed abuse towards shop workers to become so commonplace by creating more positive, respectful interactions between customers and retail staff.
“Threats, intimidation and hostility should never be accepted as simply ‘part of the job’, and we hope these figures signal that the tide may finally be beginning to turn after years of unacceptably high levels of crime and abuse so that shop staff can feel genuinely safer, more respected and properly supported.”
Matt Dawes, head of enterprise at bodycam specialist HALOS, commented: “A 2% fall in shoplifting is positive, but the headline crime figures only tell part of the story.
“The stats don’t necessarily reflect how safe retail workers feel on the shop floor or the aggression and intimidation they may face but never formally report.
“Lower retail crime figures need to translate into better experiences for employees too. Staff need to know that when something does happen, there’s a clear process for reporting it and that incidents will be taken seriously.
“Retailers need to focus on training, clear procedures and the right technology to help staff feel protected without placing the burden of intervention on them.
“Falling shoplifting figures are encouraging, but the real measure of progress is whether people on the shop floor feel safe and supported at work.”
ACS highlights increasingly violent shop theft in latest crime figures
Joanne Thomas, Usdaw general secretary, commented: “Retail crime remains at epidemic levels with over half a million shop theft incidents recorded. This is not a victimless crime.
“Dealing with repeated and persistent offences can cause issues beyond the theft itself, like anxiety, fear and physical harm to retail workers on the frontline.
“We have campaigned, along with many retail employers, for substantial legislative measures to combat this growing problem and we are pleased that the Government passed the Crime and Policing Act in April. The Act delivers a much-needed protection of retail workers law, which still needs to be brought into force, and we urge Ministers to do that as soon as possible.
“New Respect Orders for offenders, starting next week, are welcome and we hope they will be successful in changing the criminal behaviour that is blighting our shops and communities.
“The government is rebuilding neighbourhood policing. Every community has named local officers and more than 3,800 additional neighbourhood policing personnel have been delivered. They are targeting the people causing the most harm: prolific offenders, repeat offenders and organised criminal networks.
“It is welcome news that shop theft figures have fallen for the third consecutive quarter. It is our hope that these new measures will help turn the tide on shop theft and give retail staff the safe working environment they deserve.”

items.body:
With the festive season approaching and an unprecedented increase of shoppers flocking to TikTok to search for gift inspiration, brands need to maximise the platform’s growth to drive sales. New research by Bazaarvoice, the platform connecting over 13,000 brands and retailers to authentic shopper content, finds that while 66% of UK consumers now purchase goods on TikTok Shop and one in five use it at least once per week, trust remains a barrier to purchasing through the platform.
TikTok Shop is the fourth largest beauty retailer in the UK according to NielsenIQ. Last month, Boots joined the likes of Sephora and Marks & Spencer to sell their products on the platform, saying it would “bring trusted beauty expertise to a new generation of social shoppers.”
Bazaarvoice’s research shows that three quarters of shoppers have bought a product on TikTok Shop that they wouldn’t have considered buying elsewhere, and almost two thirds (64%) use the platform to discover new brands and trends.
With this in mind, it is easy to see why so many retailers and brands are choosing the social media giant to market their products for sale.
The research delves further into why consumers choose certain products and brands over others. Tellingly, 68% of shoppers are more likely to trust an everyday customer than an influencer when making a purchase on the platform.
When asked about the most important factor in their buying decision, three quarters (74%) of TikTok shoppers said star ratings and customer reviews were most important, followed by 56% who cited customer photos and videos, and just 31% who stated influencer endorsements.
David McIntosh, general manager EMEA at Bazaarvoice said, “TikTok Shop creates a fantastic opportunity for retailers to reach new customers, and this research highlights that whilst shoppers discover products through creators and they look to other customers before they buy, one of the most important elements of the sales process is trust in the brand and product.
“There is a great opportunity now for brands to focus on building authentic relationships with their customers through the use of trusted user generated content, such as customer reviews and ratings, and customer photos and videos. Actions like this could go a long way to turning prospective shoppers into long-term customers.”
Additional findings from the research include:
- 40% of shoppers are triggered to purchase on TikTok Shop by creator content
- 47% of shoppers would be more likely to shop with TikTok Shop than a traditional retailer if there was authentic video proof of the product
- 99% of respondents said they trust customer written reviews, photos and videos when making a decision to purchase

items.body:
Specialist Snowsport retailer Snow+Rock, a brand with Cotswold Outdoor Group, is celebrating raising over £50,000 for youth charity Snow Camp since January 2025. The funds will help 500 young people from inner-city and disadvantaged communities take part in Snow Camp’s First Tracks programme and experience skiing and snowboarding for the very first time.
The funds have been raised through donations from Snow+Rock’s customers, who have been invited to round up their purchases at the checkout to support Snow Camp’s important work with young people.
The programme aims to make snowsports accessible to young people who might otherwise be unable to experience them. Through combining time on the slopes with classroom-based life-skills sessions, Snow Camp’s First Tracks is designed to build confidence, develop essential life skills, and open new opportunities.
Upon completion, participants receive an accredited Snow Life Award. For many, First Tracks marks the start of a longer snowsport journey, with opportunities to progress through Snow Camp’s intermediate and advanced programmes, gain further qualifications, access apprenticeships and explore future careers within the industry.
Sharing their experience, one Snow Camp graduate commented, “Before joining Snow Camp, I wasn’t in a very good place, and I often found it difficult to step outside my comfort zone. Being part of the programme encouraged me to challenge myself, take on new opportunities, and believe in my own abilities. It has helped me become more confident, more motivated, and given me goals to work towards, including becoming a qualified snowboard instructor.”
The partnership reflects Snow+Rock’s commitment to supporting the wider snowsports community. By giving customers a simple way to contribute at checkout, the retailer is helping Snow Camp create opportunities that extend far beyond the slopes.
Jamie Kristow, CEO at Cotswold Outdoor Group said, “We are incredibly proud to have raised over £50,000 for Snow Camp since January 2025, and we are so grateful to our generous customers for making this possible. Our partnership with Snow Camp is hugely valued at Snow+Rock. Together, we are making a positive impact on the snowsports industry and helping to make snowsports more accessible to the next generation.”
Dan Charlish, founder of Snow Camp, added, “When we first discussed what might be possible between Snow Camp and Snow+Rock many years ago, we could never have imagined the partnership evolving to what it is today.
To be where we are now with the Pennies campaign – collecting donations across all Snow+Rock stores – is truly remarkable; changing young lives and laying the foundations for even greater things to come.
On behalf of everyone involved with Snow Camp, we couldn’t be more grateful to the entire Snow+Rock team for their ongoing support.”

items.title: Aldi and Lidl will be subject to same rules as major supermarkets
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has decided that Aldi, Lidl GB and Lidl NI will be designated as ‘Large Grocery Retailers’ (LGRs) under the Groceries Market Investigation (Controlled Land) Order 2010. The Order has applied to Asda, Co‑op, Marks and Spencer, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose since 2010. The Order is designed to stop […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has decided that Aldi, Lidl GB and Lidl NI will be designated as ‘Large Grocery Retailers’ (LGRs) under the Groceries Market Investigation (Controlled Land) Order 2010.
The Order has applied to Asda, Co‑op, Marks and Spencer, Morrisons, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose since 2010. The Order is designed to stop Large Grocery Retailers from using land agreements to make it harder for rival supermarkets to open nearby – in particular through the use of restrictive covenants and exclusivity arrangements. The rules ensure supermarkets compete freely – and ultimately ensure shoppers have more choice about where to buy, and how much to pay for, their groceries.
In August, the CMA invited views on its proposal to designate Aldi, Lidl GB and Lidl NI under the Order. Interested parties including Morrisons, Waitrose and Iceland submitted their views, and all supported the CMA’s proposal. The CMA did not receive representations from Aldi, Lidl GB or Lidl NI.
Once a retailer is designated, it cannot include any prohibited restrictions in new agreements – and existing agreements can be reviewed by the CMA, on the request of interested landowners, developers, and rival supermarkets. This is the case for all designated supermarkets.
Juliette Enser, executive director for Competition Enforcement and Markets at the CMA, said: “We put in place rules to stop big supermarket chains from blocking rival stores opening in their area, and now those rules apply to Aldi and Lidl.
“This will help level the playing field and make sure shoppers get the best choice of products and prices in their area.”
The UK food and grocery market is worth an estimated £222.7 billion, with Aldi and Lidl ranking among the top 5 retailers by market share.
For more information, read the CMA’s final decisions report and supporting documents on the case page.

items.title: Primark engages ‘simulation’ tech to improve supply chain decisions

The engagement begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing teams to test alternative operating configurations before […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
Primark has partnered with Kallikor, the supply chain network design platform, to introduce a simulation-led approach to significant strategic supply chain decisions. The partnership strengthens how Primark tests and validates operational and capital changes before implementation.
The engagement begins with creating digital twins of Primark’s distribution centres, allowing teams to test alternative operating configurations before implementation. By comparing scenarios in a simulated environment, Primark can identify more efficient approaches while protecting customer service and avoiding downstream cost or operational impacts across the store estate.
Adam Hoccom, director of supply chain at Primark, said: “As Primark continues to grow across markets, ensuring our supply chain is designed to support that ambition is critical. A key part of that is making sure our distribution centres operate efficiently while remaining aligned to store needs. Working with Kallikor allows us to test and compare different operating configurations – from layout and flow changes within sites to broader network considerations – before we commit capital spend.
This gives us greater confidence in the choices we make and how they will perform in practice, strengthening our ability to innovate and make well-informed decisions as we evolve our network.”
By modelling operational flows in detail – from pick paths and labour constraints to throughput variability and service impacts – Primark can see how proposed changes will perform in practice before they are introduced. The models are built from Primark’s operational data, ensuring outcomes reflect how the system actually performs under a range of real operating conditions rather than relying on assumptions or averaged views of the network.
The modelling also establishes a living decision environment built on Primark’s operational data that can be reused and extended as new strategic questions arise. Rather than commissioning a new analysis for each decision, teams can continuously test alternatives within the same validated model as the supply chain evolves.
Through simulation and AI-enabled scenario exploration, Primark teams can run and compare multiple operating futures side-by-side – assessing trade-offs across cost, service, capacity and risk in parallel. This ensures that viable options are explored comprehensively and that the strongest strategic path is chosen with clarity and confidence. It also provides a shared, system-wide evidence base that supports confident cross-functional alignment around significant strategic choices.
Jack O’Connell, CEO & co-founder of Kallikor, said: “At Primark’s scale, no supply chain decision exists in isolation. A change in one distribution centre can affect capacity, flow, service and performance across the wider network. Our role is to help teams explore decisions that would otherwise carry too much uncertainty, testing different scenarios before implementation so leaders can understand the trade-offs and move forward with confidence.
We’re proud to support Primark as they build a simulation-led decision-making capability, beginning with their distribution centres and creating the foundations for better decisions across the wider supply chain over time.”
While the initial focus is on distribution centre configuration, the modelling environment is designed to be reused as new questions arise – allowing teams to test automation pathways, capital investments, network design changes and future growth scenarios within the same validated system.
The partnership represents a step toward a more evidence-led approach to supply chain decision-making – ensuring that future growth and investment choices can be tested against operational reality before change is locked in.

items.summary: Lewisham’s £1.5bn shopping centre redevelopment freeze, caused by a breakdown between Landsec and the Council, has left residents, traders, and the town centre stranded in uncertainty, says Sergiy Lesyk Lewisham shows how a council can lose a £1.5bn scheme and gain nothing. Landsec, the property company that has owned Lewisham Shopping Centre for more than [...]
items.body:
Landsec’s blocked £.5bn shopping centre plan leaves Lewisham in the worst of all worlds
Lewisham’s £1.5bn shopping centre redevelopment freeze, caused by a breakdown between Landsec and the Council, has left residents, traders, and the town centre stranded in uncertainty, says Sergiy Lesyk
Lewisham shows how a council can lose a £1.5bn scheme and gain nothing.
Landsec, the property company that has owned Lewisham Shopping Centre for more than 20 years, has put its £1.5bn redevelopment of the centre on hold. Councillors approved the scheme in October 2025, and work had been due to start in 2027. Now nobody can say when, or whether, anything will happen.
You don’t have to have liked the plans to see the problem that residents and traders in Lewisham now face.
Landsec gave two reasons: one was the cost of building in London, the other was the Council. In Landsec’s words, recent statements from the Council “make clear that the administration is not able to support the next phase of land assembly needed to unlock delivery without a significant increase in affordable housing.”
On a social video, the mayor, Liam Shrivastava, had the temerity to state “the conditions for such developments are simply not favourable right now”, and that “the way out of the housing crisis is through building social housing.”
The mayor was elected on a promise of 1,000 new social rent homes. Instead, the plan to replace the shopping centre with 1,744 homes, including 98 for social rent and 231 at discounted rents or for key workers, will no longer be built. The shopping centre development took about five years to approve, so who really thinks this council will match it any time soon?
Boots has left its high street unit, which sits in the first phase, for a unit inside the centre. Marks & Spencer, a fixture in Lewisham for almost a century, has closed for good, Natwest has said it will close its branch, and the Model Market food hall still hasn’t reopened.
Landsec itself says the 1970s building is no longer fit for purpose, as it had been expected to be demolished.
Labour, which approved the scheme, and the Greens, who now run the Council, are busy blaming each other, and the mayor is blaming the government. Finger-pointing won’t build a single home or fill a single empty unit.
Lewisham is being let down
And the drift goes well beyond the shopping centre. A short walk away, the 649 homes of the Filigree at Lewisham Gateway have stood empty since a flood in February 2025, and residents won’t be back before October 2027. Nearby, one resident told us that food waste bins turned up at their block with no guidance and no collections. The building manager has had to tell everyone not to use them until the council explains what happens next. Even the council’s own website can’t seem to agree on whether flats are getting food waste collections.
This matters well beyond SE13. London needs homes, and it needs investors with the long-term support and confidence of local councils to build them.
So what should happen now?
First, the council should be straight with residents about what it told Landsec and what it now expects to happen to the site.
Second, it should publish a support plan for the traders caught up in the uncertainty, because they’re paying for decisions they didn’t make.
Third, and most importantly, it should set out its own plan for Lewisham town centre. If this scheme wasn’t good enough, the Council needs to show what would be, who will build it, and when.
Lewisham Conservatives support homes and investment in Lewisham, but not a town centre left in limbo. Residents were promised new homes, a new town centre and a new community. They’ve been let down. The council can’t build any of it until it first rebuilds their trust.
Sergiy Lesyk is chairman of Lewisham Conservatives

items.body:
Waitrose today opens a brand-new 18,000sq ft ‘Home of Food Lovers’ store in Cricklewood, North West London – the grocer’s first full line supermarket opening in eight years.
The next Waitrose supermarket opening will be in Hale Barns, Greater Manchester, this November.
Today the grocer has also announced the acquisition of four new sites which underpin its approach to having the right store in the right location. Joining the two new supermarkets will be a new neighbourhood store in Oakham (Rutland) and three new convenience stores in Bedminster (Bristol), Chalk Farm (London) and Springstead Village (Cambridge) which will open from 2027.
Waitrose operates three main types of store with the size, layout and ranging tailored to local needs. Small convenience stores in busy urban areas focus on fresh top-up items and quick, on-the-go purchases. Mid-size ‘neighbourhood’ stores in suburban areas carry over 6,500 products, making them ideal for everything from quick drop-ins to weekly shops. Larger supermarkets serve as destination stores with room to showcase the full breadth of the Waitrose range and concepts.
The announcements form part of Waitrose’s £1 billion multi-year investment plan, which includes expansion, store updates and the growth of its online and wholesale channels, to provide the best experience for customers.
Waitrose Cricklewood
The Cricklewood shop marks the next phase in rolling out Waitrose’s ‘Home of Food Lovers’ concept – first trialled in Newbury and now serving as the blueprint for new openings and refurbishments, adapted to suit each local community.
Central to the offering is Waitrose’s approach to quality, food integrity and animal welfare. Key features include dedicated meat, fish and sushi counters, dry-aged beef cabinet, hand-cut and speciality cheeses, on-site bakery, Fine & Rare wine selection and a fruit and veg section championing organic, Fairtrade, and regeneratively-farmed produce.
Behind the experience is a team of Partners who’ve completed extensive training to help customers discover what’s on offer. Partners in Beers, Wines & Spirits, Bakery and Counters have also completed additional training and qualifications through organisations including the Wine & Spirit Education Trust, Guild of Fine Food and specialist suppliers such as Dovecote Park and Pilgrims.
The team includes 69 new Partners who join 53 experienced team members as co-owners in the John Lewis Partnership. Three appointments were made through the Partnership’s Building Happier Futures programme, which delivers tailored support, job shadowing, and long-term career pathways for care-experienced young people.
Tina Mitchell, Waitrose retail director, said: “Our supermarkets provide the ultimate showcase for everything that sets Waitrose apart – from our unmatched quality and industry-leading welfare standards to the expert service of our Partners.
“Opening Cricklewood as our first new full-line supermarket in eight years marks an important step in bringing Waitrose closer to more communities. We continue to invest in the right shops in the right locations alongside delivering the experience customers expect from Waitrose through our online offering and wider network.”
Nationwide investment
Waitrose’s investment programme includes 29 store refurbishments this year alone and alongside today’s four new store announcements, the grocer continues work on previously announced sites – a convenience store in Ascot (Berkshire) and a 30,000 sq ft shop in Brabazon (Bristol).
To support existing stores and unlock further growth, Waitrose will open its first South West distribution centre in Avonmouth early next year.

items.title: Christmas food price rises won't be as bad as feared, says Sainsbury's boss
items.summary: The boss of Sainsbury's has said consumers will be spared dramatic price rises this Christmas but reiterated calls for the Government to relieve pressure on businesses.
items.body:
Christmas food price rises won't be as bad as feared, says Sainsbury's boss
The boss of Sainsbury's has said consumers will be spared dramatic price rises this Christmas but reiterated calls for the Government to relieve pressure on businesses.
Simon Roberts said food inflation had not 'moved anything like' the dire levels predicted by the wider industry in the immediate outbreak of the Middle East conflict.
The Food and Drink Federation's forecasts saw food inflation topping 9 per cent by the end of the year, but prices were unchanged at 1.3 per cent in the year to September, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics.
But the supermarket boss urged the Government to keep pressures on the cost of food and employment down.
In a pre-Budget plea, Roberts urged the Chancellor to use next week’s Budget to support businesses instead of ‘adding further taxes or further regulatory impacts to an industry that’s already very heavily taxed.’
Sainsbury's Simon Roberts said food inflation had not reached anywhere near levels predicted by industry gr
He said that the shock increase in National Insurance contributions had increased costs in the retail and hospitality sectors and the Government should ‘make sure we don't do anything to further aggravate that situation.’
Defending reports of supermarkets’ pleas to be excluded from high business rates, Roberts said that retail is ‘one of the highest taxed sectors’ and includes major employers which employ millions of people.
The Chancellor last week met with bosses from Morrisons, Sainsbury's and Tesco, where Roberts said he felt 'heard'.
The remarks from the chief executive came as Britain’s second biggest grocer upgraded its annual profit forecasts and said customers will not ‘trade down’ this Christmas despite economic pressures.
The group had been forecasting profits between £965 million and £1.065 billion but raised this to a range between £1.025 billion and £1.065billion - after the impact of the war in the Middle East had taken less of a toll than feared.
The grocer said booming sales of its own-label premium Taste The Difference ranges helped grocery sales rise 2.9 per cent to £13.2 billion.
Customers were ‘planning early’ for the festive season, with Sainsbury's adding more online grocery shops to keep up with demand.
Roberts added: ‘I think [what] will be a real theme into Christmas, is customers don't want to trade down. They want the best value and the best quality, and that's really what we are focused on.’
There had been ‘a lot of concern earlier in the year as to where food inflation might go,’ Roberts said, but ‘actually [it] has yet to see much of a move’.
But he said there was ‘pressure’ in the system heading into the autumn and winter, including fertiliser prices and energy costs. ‘We’re going to be doing what we’ve done consistently, working really hard to give customers the value that they expect,’ he said.
But shares tumbled 3 per cent after Sainsbury's revealed slower sales growth.
Lucy Rumbold, equity research analyst at Quilter, said: 'It’s worth noting that inflationary pressures stemming from developments in the Middle East have taken longer than initially expected to feed across European markets.
'Grocers such as Sainsbury’s have therefore kept price growth below headline inflation to protect their value proposition, which has seemingly weighed on like-for-like sales. However, this as a sensible strategy.
'If Sainsbury’s continues to resonate with households on value for money, it should be well positioned to benefit as inflation is eventually passed through. We expect this to become more evident towards year-end, as higher fertiliser costs feed through and lower-cost inventory is depleted.'
