items.body:
Waitrose has launched Leckford Single Estate Gin and Leckford Single Estate Vodka, the first spirits made from crops grown on a UK supermarket’s own farm.
Both spirits are distilled from grain, but it is unusual to know which farm, let alone which field or day it was harvested. These came from a single field at the Waitrose Farm at Leckford in Hampshire, harvested on 10 July, and reached Waitrose shelves just over three months later, in time for Christmas.
The wheat was grown using regenerative practices, which seek to restore the soil, conserve water and support biodiversity. For the spirits, the field grew oilseed rape the year before, was never left bare between harvests, and the seed was sown into narrow strips rather than ploughing the whole field. Both spirits carry Waitrose’s Championing Regenerative Farming logo, which also appears on Waitrose’s own-label milk and shows products from farms using these practices.
It is the first time the estate has grown a crop specifically for spirits. Leckford wheat has gone into Leckford Homebaking flour since 2003 and Leckford bread since 2024, but this year the Leckford team grew three new varieties as a bespoke spirit grain, chosen with Ramsbury, the Wiltshire estate distillery that made the gin and vodka.
Leckford is where Waitrose has farmed to regenerative principles since 2020. It works closely with farmers and growers, supporting Waitrose Farming for Nature programme, a commitment for all its UK farmers and growers to have started using regenerative practices by 2030.
Regenerative farming also depends on farmers being able to sell what they grow. When it launched Farming for Nature in 2024, Waitrose committed to providing a market for regeneratively produced food, and the spirits give Leckford’s wheat a new one. They take the Leckford range to 17 products, alongside the estate’s bread, flour, oil and honey for food lovers who want to know exactly where their food comes from.
The spirits are the latest in a line of firsts from Leckford. Vines planted there in 2009 made Waitrose the first UK retailer with its own vineyard and the first supermarket to sell its own English sparkling wine. In 2023 it became the first UK retailer to run tractors on renewable natural gas. And in 2024 Leckford’s vineyard and orchards became the first in the UK to gain Regenified certification, an independent standard for regenerative farming.
The wheat is distilled in small batches at Ramsbury, which runs on renewable energy. The gin takes its inspiration from the wild plants that grow across the estate. Its 11 botanicals include juniper, sweet orange, lemon and warming cinnamon. The vodka is distilled four times for a smooth texture with notes of caramel and vanilla. The harvest made 30,000 bottles, on sale now in over 200 Waitrose shops at £25 each.
Andrew Hoad, director of the Leckford Estate and Farming for Nature at Waitrose, said: “We’ve grown wheat for baking at Leckford for more than twenty years, but this is the first time we’ve grown it for spirits. Our commitment to regenerative farming reflects the belief that producing high-quality food and caring for the environment go hand in hand, and these spirits are a taste of exactly that.”
Nik Fordham, Master Distiller and general manager at Ramsbury, said: “Distilling grain grown on a single farm gives us an incredible level of connection to the raw material and the land it comes from. Working with the team at Leckford, we were able to select wheat varieties specifically for their suitability for distilling, considering how their characteristics would influence the flavour, texture and quality of the finished spirits. The choice of grain is fundamental to what we make, and being involved from the field through to distillation allows us to understand and celebrate that journey. It’s a great example of what can be achieved when farming and distilling expertise come together, creating spirits with a genuine sense of place and a clear connection to the land.”

items.title: Fix 'broken' business rates system once and for all, Chancellor told in letter from 200 bosses
items.summary: More than 200 employers have called on the Chancellor to tear up the 'broken' business rates system to revive Britain's battered high streets.
items.body:
Fix 'broken' business rates system once and for all, Chancellor told in letter from 200 bosses
More than 200 employers have called on the Chancellor to tear up the 'broken' business rates system to revive Britain's battered high streets.
In a letter to John Healey ahead of the Budget, the business leaders warn the levy is holding back investment, jobs and growth by placing a 'disproportionate burden' on physical stores.
They argue that 'piecemeal' changes – such as support for pubs proposed by Andy Burnham – have created an increasingly complicated system that 'picks winners and losers without ever fixing the underlying problem'.
The letter – whose signatories range from hotelier Sir Rocco Forte and the bosses of Boodles and The Ritz to galleries and the owners of nurseries and cafes – calls on the government to adopt a new 'hybrid' model involving a 2 per cent levy on online sales and a 37 per cent cut for bricks-and-mortar firms.
Forte, chairman of Rocco Forte Hotels, said: 'Hotels are facing average business rates increases of 115 per cent over the next three years, a level that will be unsustainable for some and will inevitably kill investment and jobs.
'We need fundamental reform, not another round of piecemeal reliefs for a few sectors. The hybrid business rate offers a practical way to create a fairer system which ensures online businesses make their contribution and reduces the burden on businesses that invest in physical premises.'
New Chancellor John Healey has been urged to fix the 'broken' business rates system following the botched reforms of his predecessor Rachel Reeves
Sir Rocco Forte is among the business leaders calling for reform
Michael Wainwright, managing director of Boodles, a family-owned jeweller for six generations, said: 'Businesses that invest in bricks and mortar, employ people and contribute to the life of our high streets should not carry a disproportionate share of the tax burden simply because they have physical premises.
'At Boodles, our stores are an important part of how we engage with customers and showcase British design and craftsmanship, but the cost of occupying those premises is a significant fixed cost.'
The intervention – less than two weeks ahead of the Budget on October 28 – underlines the anger among business chiefs over Rachel Reeves' botched reforms of the rates system.
Having pledged to level the playing field between the high street and online rivals, the former Chancellor hammered business with a spiralling rates bill.
Business leaders are now calling on Burnham and Healey to act – though it is feared the Chancellor will instead announce support for the high street rather than fundamental reform.
The letter, which was organised by the Real Rates Reform Alliance and brings together senior figures from retail and hospitality to tourism, property and leisure, said: 'We welcomed the recent announcement by the Prime Minister to cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
'However, while this decision recognises some of the inadequacies within the current business rates system, it is not the fundamental change required to fix this broken system once and for all.
'We believe this moment now presents a unique opportunity to go further and create a business tax system that fixes the current regime's fundamental imbalances, supports firms across all sectors and drives investment in communities and long-term economic growth.'
It concludes: 'Britain has spent three decades adjusting business rates instead of resolving their fundamental flaws. The time has come to modernise this broken system.
'We call on you to seize this opportunity to create a business tax system that is simpler, fairer, more sustainable, and better aligned with the economy of the future.'
Ros Morgan, chairman of the Real Rates Reform Alliance, said: 'This letter shows that business rates reform is a concern across every sector of business and right across the UK. Businesses recognise that the current system is holding back investment, growth and jobs.
'Decades of piecemeal reliefs have failed to fix the underlying problem. The Government now has an opportunity to deliver fundamental reform rather than simply move the burden between sectors.
'The hybrid business rate would cut the burden on businesses investing in physical places while broadening the tax base. With the Budget approaching, the Chancellor should seize this opportunity to deliver lasting reform.'
Boodles managing director Michael Wainwright, whose jewellery has been modelled by Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer
Helen Swaby, chief executive of Clarendon Fine Art, said: 'With more than 90 galleries, our physical presence is at the heart of what we do. Business rates are therefore a significant and unavoidable cost.
'We need a system that recognises the value bricks-and-mortar businesses bring to our high streets and town centres, rather than placing a disproportionate burden on those that invest in them.
'If we want thriving town centres and successful businesses across the country, we need a rates system that supports investment in physical places as part of thriving communities.'
Anda Rowland, director of Anderson & Sheppard, tailors to the King, said: 'Business rates are not an abstract tax for a business like ours.
'We employ highly skilled people and invest in training the next generation of craftspeople, but every increase in the cost of our premises puts greater pressure on our ability to invest in those people and in the future of the business.
'We need a business rates system that recognises the value created by businesses that invest in people, skills and physical places.'
The letter sent to the Chancellor
Dear Chancellor,
Across the UK, too many towns and cities are being held back from realising their economic potential.
In 2024 alone, almost 13,000 shops closed (around 37 every day), as rising costs continued to outpace growth.
Businesses that invest in communities create jobs, drive productivity and sustain local economies, yet the current business rates system places a disproportionate burden on those businesses, while an increasing share of economic activity now takes place online without making a proportional contribution to the tax base.
Against this backdrop, we welcomed the recent announcement by the Prime Minister to cut business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.
However, while this decision recognises some of the inadequacies within the current business rates system, it is not the fundamental change required to fix this broken system once and for all.
We believe this moment now presents a unique opportunity to go further and create a business tax system that fixes the current regime's fundamental imbalances, support firms across all sectors and drive investment in communities and long-term economic growth.
For more than two decades, governments of all colours have sought to reform business rates through new reliefs, exemptions and differential multipliers for individual sectors.
While often well-intentioned, this piecemeal approach has produced an excessively complex set of reliefs and special provisions that picks winners and losers without ever fixing the underlying problem.
The result is a fundamentally flawed system that is harder to understand, less economically rational and increasingly disconnected from the way the modern economy operates.
The next phase of business rates reform should build upon sector-specific interventions and modernise the system itself. The tax system should better reflect where economic activity takes place.
We therefore urge you to consider a fundamental reset, of the sort Labour promised in opposition.
We believe the Hybrid Business Rate is the comprehensive reform that this moment requires.
It combines a lower property-based business rate with a modest levy on eligible online sales across the economy.
The levy would be collected through the existing tax system, using an established administrative mechanism that minimises additional costs for businesses and government.
Broadening the tax base in this way would generate sufficient revenue to reduce business rates by up to 37 per cent, while maintaining sustainable funding for local government.
Carefully designed exemptions would ensure that the levy applies only to eligible online sales, protects small businesses and continues to support investment in physical places and experiences.
A Hybrid Business Rate is more than a reform of business rates. It is a modern fiscal framework designed for today's economy, one that supports investment and provides combined authorities with a broader and more resilient tax base to underpin devolution, infrastructure, and long-term place-based growth.
Britain has spent three decades adjusting business rates instead of resolving their fundamental flaws. The time has come to modernise this broken system.
We call on you to seize this opportunity to create a business tax system that is simpler, fairer, more sustainable, and better aligned with the economy of the future.
